meta.label: Electricity suppliers
tradeoffLabels: lowest bill, protected by the price cap
meta.attribution: Covers domestic electricity suppliers in Great Britain, meaning England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has separate energy regulation and is not included here. Renewable share and fuel mix figures come from each supplier's own Ofgem-mandated Fuel Mix Disclosure, published every October (April 2025 to March 2026 where a supplier has published it), or from Citizens Advice's compiled fuel mix data where a supplier's own disclosure page could not be read directly. Customer service scores come from the Citizens Advice Energy Supplier Star Rating for April to June 2026, compiled by Citizens Advice as the statutory consumer advocate for energy, not by a switching site, and are its overall rating out of 5 multiplied by 20. Only the main table, which covers suppliers with more than 25,000 customer accounts, is scored: Citizens Advice calculates a separate rating for smaller suppliers that it says cannot be compared with the main table, so those suppliers are left unscored on service and their rating is mentioned in the description instead. A brand supplied under another company's licence is scored on that supplier's rating where Citizens Advice says so; brands with no Citizens Advice rating are left unscored on service. A tariff marketed as '100 per cent renewable' is usually backed by Renewable Energy Guarantees of Origin (REGO) certificates bought separately from the electricity itself, which on their own do not prove the supplier funded new renewable generation. Ofgem has recognized only three suppliers, Ecotricity, Good Energy and 100Green (formerly Green Energy UK), as giving renewable generation support beyond what subsidies and obligations already require, and has exempted their tariffs from the price cap on that basis. Every other supplier's renewable tariff here relies on REGO certificates unless its own page says otherwise. Prices change every three months with the Ofgem price cap and vary by region and payment method; check a supplier's current Tariff Information Label before switching. Community energy schemes and home solar generation are separate decisions in this catalogue. Suggest changes via Contribute.

products.name: British Gas
products.description: The largest domestic electricity and gas supplier in Great Britain, owned by Centrica. Its standard tariffs sit at the regulated price cap, and its dedicated renewable product is backed by REGO certificates rather than new generation.

price.note: British Gas's standard variable and default electricity tariffs cannot charge more than the level Ofgem sets and updates every three months under the energy price cap.

environment.note: British Gas Trading Limited's Fuel Mix Disclosure for April 2025 to March 2026 was 45 per cent renewable, 46 per cent nuclear, 7 per cent natural gas and 1 per cent coal, giving 91 per cent zero carbon electricity against a UK average of 62 per cent; its renewable share remains just below the 48 per cent UK average.

transparency.note: British Gas's own energy sources page explains that for some tariffs suppliers own or buy Renewable Energy Guarantees of Origin certificates to show that customers' electricity was sourced from renewables, and that electricity from a particular generator cannot be traced to a customer's home.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave British Gas an overall star rating of 2.61 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 14th of the 16 suppliers in its main table, with a complaints rate of 68.8 per 10,000 customers, its weakest scoring category.

products.name: EDF Energy
products.description: A large supplier whose electricity is mostly nuclear rather than renewable. It markets zero carbon and renewable products, but its public fuel mix page does not explain how the renewable claim is backed.

price.note: EDF's default electricity tariff is bound by the same Ofgem price cap as every supplier without a derogation.

environment.note: EDF Energy Customers Limited's fuel mix for April 2025 to March 2026 was 41.1 per cent nuclear, 28.5 per cent gas, 23.0 per cent renewables, 5.0 per cent coal and 2.4 per cent other, against a 48 per cent UK renewable average.

transparency.note: EDF's fuel mix page breaks its mix down by product, showing its renewable products at 100 per cent renewable and everything else at 7.7 per cent, but unlike British Gas's equivalent page it does not explain REGO certificates or how the renewable claim is backed.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave EDF Energy an overall star rating of 2.96 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 10th of the 16 suppliers in its main table.

products.name: Octopus Energy
products.description: A fast-growing independent supplier reporting the highest renewable share of the mainstream suppliers in this list, with billions of pounds committed to wind, solar and battery projects it owns or has long-term contracts with.

price.note: Octopus Energy's headline tariffs are bound by the Ofgem price cap in the same way as other suppliers without a derogation.

environment.note: Octopus reports a fuel mix of 86.4 per cent renewables and 13.6 per cent nuclear for April 2024 to March 2025, and says it has put 6 billion pounds into around 4GW of renewable projects it owns or holds long-term contracts with, plus a further 15 billion pound commitment toward 12GW of offshore wind by 2030.

transparency.note: Octopus's green page explains that renewable and other generators all feed the same National Grid, and that it matches customer usage to renewable generation through Power Purchase Agreements with more than 700 UK generators rather than delivering separate electrons to each home.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave Octopus Energy an overall star rating of 3.67 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 5th of the 16 suppliers in its main table.

products.name: OVO Energy
products.description: OVO stopped buying standard renewable certificates in 2023, so its headline fuel mix disclosure looks low. Its Greener Electricity option buys power directly from renewable generators, for an added fee.

price.note: OVO's standard tariffs sit under the same Ofgem price cap as other non-derogated suppliers, and OVO charges 7.62 pounds a month to add its Greener Electricity upgrade, of which it says 40 pounds a year goes to helping new independent renewable generators get started.

environment.note: OVO says it stopped buying standard REGO certificates in 2023, so its disclosed fuel mix for April 2025 to March 2026 is only 12 per cent renewable against a 48 per cent UK average; it says it buys electricity for its Greener Electricity customers directly from renewable generators and invests in new independent renewable power instead.

transparency.note: OVO's own fuel mix page says REGO certificates 'don't actually make the UK electricity grid any greener' and that such tariffs alone 'don't generate any more green energy or give you 100% green energy at home'.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave Ovo Energy an overall star rating of 3.65 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 6th of the 16 suppliers in its main table.

products.name: E.ON Next
products.description: E.ON Next backs its renewable electricity with a mix of E.ON's own renewable assets, agreements with independent UK generators and bought certificates, and says plainly that the electricity itself still comes from the shared National Grid.

price.note: E.ON Next's default electricity tariff sits under the Ofgem price cap along with other suppliers that hold no derogation.

environment.note: E.ON Next's fuel mix for April 2025 to March 2026 was 27.3 per cent renewable, down from 31.3 per cent the year before and well below the 48 per cent UK average, with 53.2 per cent natural gas and 9.3 per cent coal.

transparency.note: E.ON Next's tariffs page says its renewable-backed electricity is sourced from E.ON's own renewable assets, agreements with independent UK generators and the purchase of renewable electricity certificates, and states plainly that the electricity supplied to a home 'comes from the National Grid'.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave E.ON Next an overall star rating of 3.71 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 3rd of the 16 suppliers in its main table, the highest among the large suppliers descended from the Big Six.

products.name: ScottishPower
products.description: One of the long-established Big Six suppliers, owned by Iberdrola. Its published fuel mix shows one of the lowest renewable shares among the suppliers in this list.

price.note: ScottishPower's default tariff is bound by the same Ofgem price cap as other suppliers without a derogation.

environment.note: Citizens Advice records ScottishPower's fuel mix as 84 per cent fossil fuel, 7 per cent renewable, 4 per cent nuclear and 5 per cent other for the same reporting period as its January to March 2026 star rating.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave ScottishPower an overall star rating of 2.76 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 12th of the 16 suppliers in its main table, with a complaints rate of 76.4 per 10,000 customers.

products.name: Good Energy
products.description: A small independent supplier that buys power directly from more than 3,000 independent renewable generators. Ofgem has recognized its tariffs as delivering renewable support beyond subsidies, and its standard tariff is exempt from the price cap.

price.note: Ofgem has granted Good Energy an enduring exemption from the default tariff cap for its renewable Standard Variable Tariffs, and states explicitly that it has not assessed whether the exempted tariffs are good value for consumers.

environment.note: Good Energy says all its tariffs are matched with 100 per cent renewable electricity bought from more than 3,000 independent generators, and that it achieved an 87 per cent half-hourly match between customer demand and renewable generation between April 2025 and March 2026, verified by the Matched Clean Power Index.

transparency.note: Good Energy publishes its half-hourly matching percentage and the breakdown of its April 2025 to March 2026 fuel mix by technology, 55 per cent wind, 27 per cent biogeneration, 9 per cent hydro and 9 per cent solar, rather than a single headline renewable figure.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave Good Energy an overall star rating of 3.68 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 4th of the 16 suppliers in its main table.

products.name: Ecotricity
products.description: Founded in 1995 to sell green electricity as a mainstream product, Ecotricity has built its own wind and solar parks over three decades rather than only buying certificates. Its renewable tariffs are also exempt from the Ofgem price cap.

price.note: Ofgem has granted The Renewable Energy Company Limited, trading as Ecotricity, an enduring exemption from the default tariff cap for its renewable Standard Variable Tariffs, and states it has not assessed whether the exempted tariffs are good value for consumers.

environment.note: Ecotricity says it supplies 100 per cent green electricity against an industry average it puts at around 40 per cent, and that over the past 30 years it has built 24 wind parks, three solar parks and one green gasmill rather than only buying certificates.

transparency.note: Ecotricity's fuel mix page shows a 100 per cent renewable disclosure for 2025/26 drawn from offshore wind, onshore wind, solar and hydro, but does not break down what share of customer supply comes from the parks it has built against electricity it buys in.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave Ecotricity an overall star rating of 3.40 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 8th of the 16 suppliers in its main table.

links.label: How much green energy Ecotricity generates

products.name: 100Green
products.description: Formerly Green Energy UK, 100Green buys electricity through Power Purchase Agreements with independent generators and holds a REGO certificate for every unit it supplies, audited annually by Ofgem. It is one of three suppliers Ofgem has exempted from the price cap for genuine additionality.

price.note: Ofgem has granted Green Energy UK Plc, now trading as 100Green, an enduring exemption from the default tariff cap for its renewable Standard Variable Tariffs, and states it has not assessed whether the exempted tariffs are good value for consumers.

environment.note: 100Green's own energy page shows a 100 per cent renewable electricity fuel mix for April 2024 to March 2025, and its FAQ explains that it buys power through Power Purchase Agreements with independent generators rather than generating its own.

transparency.note: 100Green's FAQ explains in plain terms what a Power Purchase Agreement and a REGO certificate are, states it holds a REGO for every megawatt hour it supplies, and says the certification process is audited annually by Ofgem.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave 100Green an overall star rating of 3.90 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 2nd of the 16 suppliers in its main table, second only to Outfox Energy.

products.name: Utility Warehouse
products.description: A telecoms and insurance bundler that also sells energy. Its own fuel mix disclosure shows only 11 per cent renewable electricity for April 2025 to March 2026; a fully green tariff is sold separately as an add-on.

price.note: Utility Warehouse's electricity tariff is bound by the same Ofgem price cap as other suppliers without a derogation.

environment.note: Utility Warehouse's own fuel mix disclosure for April 2025 to March 2026 shows 65 per cent gas, 11 per cent coal, 7 per cent nuclear and 11 per cent renewable, with emissions of about 396g of carbon dioxide per kWh.

transparency.note: Utility Warehouse's fuel mix page states its percentages plainly, including the low renewable share, without offering a REGO or certificate explanation.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave Utility Warehouse an overall star rating of 2.63 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 13th of the 16 suppliers in its main table.

products.name: Utilita
products.description: A supplier built around prepayment meters and smart pay-as-you-go billing. It does not market a green tariff and says publicly that no supplier can honestly claim a 100 per cent renewable tariff, a position its own fuel mix disclosure supports.

price.note: Utilita's electricity tariffs sit under the same Ofgem price cap as other suppliers without a derogation.

environment.note: Citizens Advice records Utilita's fuel mix as 83 per cent fossil fuel, 11 per cent nuclear, 0 per cent renewable and 7 per cent other on the page showing its April to June 2026 star rating; Citizens Advice does not state which disclosure year the mix covers.

transparency.note: Utilita's own sustainability page says 'no matter what suppliers say, there's no such thing as a 100 per cent renewable tariff' because every household draws from the same National Grid, and the company does not market a green tariff.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave Utilita an overall star rating of 2.53 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 15th of the 16 suppliers in its main table, with a complaints rate of 95.7 per 10,000 customers.

products.name: So Energy
products.description: An independent supplier whose disclosed fuel mix is well above the national average for renewables. Its own page explaining how that share is sourced could not be read directly for this entry, so only the disclosed figures are scored here.

price.note: So Energy's electricity tariffs are bound by the same Ofgem price cap as other suppliers without a derogation.

environment.note: Citizens Advice records So Energy's fuel mix as 67 per cent renewable, 27 per cent fossil fuel, 4 per cent nuclear and 2 per cent other on the page showing its April to June 2026 star rating; Citizens Advice does not state which disclosure year the mix covers.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave So Energy an overall star rating of 2.85 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 11th of the 16 suppliers in its main table.

products.name: Outfox Energy
products.description: A Leicester-based budget supplier trading as Outfox Energy, formerly Outfox the Market. Its licence is held by Foxglove Energy Supply Ltd, the company Ofgem fined 1.8 million pounds in 2023 for repeatedly failing to submit financial data, owned since 2024 by Bastian Holdings Limited. A separate, dormant company named Outfox the Market Limited was dissolved in July 2026 without affecting supply. Its customer service ranked first in Citizens Advice's April to June 2026 table.

price.note: Outfox Energy's tariffs are bound by the same Ofgem price cap as other suppliers without a derogation.

environment.note: Citizens Advice records Outfox Energy's fuel mix as 41 per cent renewable, 43 per cent fossil fuel, 14 per cent nuclear and 3 per cent other on the page showing its April to June 2026 star rating; Citizens Advice does not state which disclosure year the mix covers.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave Outfox Energy an overall star rating of 4.03 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 1st of the 16 suppliers in its main table, the top of its table, with a complaints rate of 17.9 per 10,000 customers.

links.label: Companies House: Foxglove Energy Supply ownership

products.name: TruEnergy
products.description: A small supplier that Ofgem ordered in 2022 to audit and correct how it sets customers' direct debits. It ranks last on Citizens Advice's quarterly supplier table and discloses one of the lowest renewable shares in this list.

price.note: TruEnergy's tariffs are bound by the same Ofgem price cap as other suppliers without a derogation.

environment.note: Citizens Advice records TruEnergy's fuel mix as 8 per cent renewable, 76 per cent fossil fuel, 10 per cent nuclear and 6 per cent other on the page showing its April to June 2026 star rating; Citizens Advice does not state which disclosure year the mix covers.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave TruEnergy an overall star rating of 1.38 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 16th of the 16 suppliers in its main table, the lowest of any supplier in its table.

products.name: Co-op Energy
products.description: Owned by the Midcounties Co-operative and run on Octopus Energy's supply licence and technology. It funds a joint venture, Younity, that has backed more than 250 community energy projects, and puts 10 pounds from every new customer into a community energy fund.

price.note: Co-op Energy is a white label brand supplied under Octopus Energy's licence and technology, so its tariffs are bound by the same Ofgem price cap as Octopus's own tariffs.

environment.note: EnergyCoop, the brand behind Co-op Energy, says it 'only provides 100 per cent renewable energy' and describes its flagship tariff as the UK's only tariff powered by 100 per cent community owned renewable energy.

transparency.note: EnergyCoop explains that its Younity joint venture with Octopus has supported more than 250 community energy projects and puts 10 pounds from every new customer into a Powering Communities Fund for community energy groups.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave EnergyCoop an overall star rating of 3.64 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ranked 7th of the 16 suppliers in its main table.

links.label: Community energy and the Octopus partnership

products.name: E (Gas and Electricity)
products.description: A Birmingham-based supplier serving more than 300,000 customers, mostly on prepayment smart meters it tops up through its own app. Its own fuel mix disclosure is mostly gas and coal, and it does not market a green tariff.

price.note: E's standard variable electricity tariffs, including prepayment, cannot charge more than the level Ofgem sets under the energy price cap, which applies for 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027 at different levels by region and payment method.

environment.note: E's own Fuel Mix Disclosure for April 2025 to March 2026 shows 65 per cent natural gas, 11 per cent coal, 7 per cent nuclear, 11 per cent renewables and 5 per cent other.

transparency.note: E's fuel mix page states its percentages plainly as the regulations require, without any explanation of REGO certificates or how renewable electricity is sourced; it does not sell a green tariff.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice gave E (Gas and Electricity) an overall star rating of 3.40 out of 5 for April to June 2026, ninth of 16, with a strong 5.0 for billing and metering but 1.5 for complaints, at 56.5 complaints per 10,000 customers.

products.name: Fuse Energy
products.description: A venture-backed newcomer that builds its own solar and wind sites and sells the renewable certificates they earn rather than using them to call its tariffs 100 per cent green. It says its variable tariffs undercut the price cap. Citizens Advice gives it a smaller-supplier rating of 3.4 out of 5 for April to June 2026, which it says is calculated differently and cannot be compared with the main table, so it is not scored here.

price.note: Fuse says its variable tariffs beat the UK price cap so that it is always cheaper than major UK suppliers; this is the company's own claim, and its tariffs remain subject to the Ofgem cap as a ceiling.

environment.note: Fuse says it generated 18.9 GWh from its own solar and wind farms between April 2024 and March 2025, about 17.5 per cent of its supply, with the remaining 82.49 per cent drawn from the grid at 246.9g of carbon dioxide per kWh; its projects page lists completed solar sites in Hampshire, Devon and Moray.

transparency.note: Fuse's fuel mix page says buying certificates to claim '100% green' is 'misleading', explains that it sells its own renewable certificates and reinvests the money in new generation, and shows its own-generation share and grid emissions instead of a certificate-backed headline figure.

products.name: Tulo Energy
products.description: A small domestic supplier trading as Tulo Energy through Square1 Energy Ltd, selling on simple pricing and quick service. Its disclosed fuel mix is almost entirely fossil fuel and it does not market a green tariff. Citizens Advice gives it a smaller-supplier rating of 3.3 out of 5 for April to June 2026, with 0 out of 5 for customer commitments; Citizens Advice says this rating cannot be compared with the main table, so it is not scored here.

price.note: Tulo Energy's standard variable tariffs are bound by the same Ofgem price cap as other suppliers without a derogation.

environment.note: Tulo's own fuel mix page for April 2024 to March 2025 shows 74.7 per cent natural gas, 14.8 per cent coal, 3.9 per cent nuclear and only 0.3 per cent renewable, against a UK average of 42.1 per cent renewable.

transparency.note: Tulo's fuel mix page sets out the regulated table plainly beside the UK average, without any explanation of REGO certificates or renewable sourcing. The page loads its figures with JavaScript and was read in a browser.

products.name: Home Energy
products.description: A small family-owned supplier, part of the Net Zero Planet Group controlled by Keith and Maria Bastian, whose family company also owns Outfox Energy's licence holder, that competes on price and says its variable tariffs have stayed under the price cap since 2019. It states a fuel mix close to the national average without saying how the renewable share is sourced. Citizens Advice gives it a smaller-supplier rating of 3.9 out of 5 for April to June 2026, with 0 out of 5 for customer commitments; Citizens Advice says this rating cannot be compared with the main table, so it is not scored here.

price.note: Home Energy's homepage shows its Fair Variable electricity-only tariff at the same price as the Ofgem cap and its dual fuel variable tariff 4.12 per cent below it, at typical use, for October 2026.

environment.note: Home Energy says 40.8 per cent of its electricity comes from renewables, 39.3 per cent from natural gas, 13.9 per cent from nuclear, 3.4 per cent from coal and 2.6 per cent from other sources.

transparency.note: Home Energy's energy page gives its fuel mix percentages without naming the reporting period or explaining whether the renewable share rests on REGO certificates or direct contracts. The page loads with JavaScript and was read in a browser.

products.name: London Power
products.description: An energy brand founded by the Mayor of London and owned by the Greater London Authority, supplied and serviced by Octopus Energy for London addresses only. It matches all customer electricity with zero-carbon generation and says it reinvests in London communities.

price.note: London Power is supplied by Octopus Energy Ltd, so its tariffs sit under the same Ofgem price cap as Octopus's own; London Power says it automatically moves customers to its cheapest similar plan when a plan ends.

environment.note: Citizens Advice records London Power's fuel mix as 100 per cent renewable, and London Power says all the electricity its customers use is matched with power from zero-carbon sources such as sun and wind, drawn from Octopus Energy's supply.

transparency.note: London Power's site says customer electricity is matched with zero-carbon generation and supplied by Octopus, but does not explain on its own pages whether that matching rests on certificates or direct contracts; Octopus's own page explains its approach.

accessibility.note: Citizens Advice says Octopus Energy provides energy and customer service for London Power and points readers to Octopus's results, which were 3.67 out of 5 for April to June 2026.

products.name: Sainsbury's Energy
products.brand: supermarket brand on E.ON Next's licence
products.description: A supermarket energy brand that pays Nectar points on bills. It is a trading name used under licence by E.ON Next, so its fuel mix and price cap position are E.ON Next's.

price.note: Sainsbury's Energy's price cap page says customers on its standard variable tariff saw unit rates and standing charges change with the Ofgem cap from 1 October 2026, set at 1,723 pounds a year for a typical Direct Debit household.

environment.note: Sainsbury's Energy's fuel mix page says its customers are supplied under E.ON Next's licence and gives E.ON Next's mix for April 2025 to March 2026 as 53.2 per cent natural gas, 27.3 per cent renewable, 9.3 per cent coal, 5.8 per cent nuclear and 4.4 per cent other, against a 48 per cent UK renewable average.

transparency.note: The fuel mix page says plainly that the figures are E.ON Next's and gives emissions per kWh, but does not explain REGO certificates or how any renewable claim is backed.
